title: The Philosophy of Liberation (Moksha Darshan): A Manual of Sant Mat Mysticism
author: Maharshi Mehi Paramhans (1885-1986)
year: Hindi original (as part four of Satsang-Yoga) 1940; English translation 1998
edition_cited: Sant Mat Society of North America, first English edition (108 copies), August 1998; archive.org item PhilosophyOfLiberationAManualOfSantMatMysticism
tradition: Santmat of Bihar (Maharshi Mehi lineage, from Tulsi Sahib via Baba Devi Sahab)
locator_hints: Numbered aphorisms. File lines 1130-1190 (printed pp. 25-26): manas japa and manas dhyan as preparation; bindu 'cannot be marked by the tip of a hair'; drishti yoga defined as 'uniting the rays of both eyes on the focus and gazing on it with a steady mind'; straining pupils or eyeballs 'brings pain and abnormality in the eyes'
File c. 1273-1310 (aphorism 68 and around): once one-pointedness is attained drop drishti yoga and take up sound; light is within the sound

Aphorisms 91-94 (file c. 1826-1845): eyes shut comfortably 'without turning the eyeballs or pressing them in any way'; times of day (3 a.m. etc.); eyes and mouth closed, ears closed only for sound practice
File c. 1870-1910: pratyahara, returning repeatedly to the focal point; 'the Divine vision dawns'
Translators' appendix (file c. 2300-2360): five-stage summary; 'One gazes into the middle of the darkness or the Light one sees'
summary: Mehi's compact manual of the four-stage Santmat sadhana: mental repetition (manas japa), visualising a holy form (manas dhyan), drishti yoga or bindu dhyana, then inner sound. The third stage is the light practice: with eyes comfortably shut, the two lines of sight are brought together on an infinitesimal point in the inner darkness and held there with a steady mind; the point cannot be imagined or marked, and is found only by this converging gaze. Mehi is unusually explicit on mechanics and prohibitions: no turning, straining or pressing of the eyeballs (which brings 'pain and abnormality'), no drowsiness, fixed daily hours. One-pointedness on the bindu opens 'subtle or divine sight' and lights appear; once established, the gaze practice should be dropped for sound, since staying with light costs time. The first two stages are presented as the preparation that makes the third possible.
why_relevant: Explicit, mechanical instruction for producing first inner light by converging the gaze on a point in closed-eye darkness, with a stated preparatory sequence and warnings against eye pressure.

notes: In copyright; uploaded by the publisher's webmaster under CC BY-NC-ND 3.0, so the full text is saved, but passages should be paraphrased with anchors. The final pages are translators' and editors' notes (James Bean), not Mehi's text: keep them distinct. The tradition requires initiation for the exact technique; the book states this.
